en: In this key, the rise in prices is compatible with a rentier rationality of maximizing dividends through markups defined by the intermediary's structural position, draining income through subscriptions, fees and access “rights”, which explains the author's refusal of the conventional monetary diagnosis and his direct criticism of the Central Bank's justifications: “It is not demand inflation, and the Central Bank's justifications […] are simply false”. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 70)</2>.

The expression “mandatory intermediary” describes, in Dowbor, the shift from competition by product to competition by infrastructural position: rentier gain stabilizes when critical layers of circulation, computing and intermediation become unavoidable points of passage, shifting the dispute to control of access. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 31)</2>.
The Amazon case illustrates this conversion of internal capacity into a generalized toll: “AWS as well as FBA are […] infrastructure rentiers.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

This position is sustained by technical and economic barriers to replication: “Amazon controls critical infrastructures […] in ways that new interested parties (entrants) would find difficult to replicate or to challenge through competition.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

The relevant legal point is that intermediation ceases to be a mere “neutral” provision and comes to operate as unilateral governance of the point of passage, with effects on continuity, conditions of permanence and the power to impose recurring costs in dependent digital ecosystems. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

Dowbor offers a systemic frame for contemporary rentierism by emphasizing the mismatch between the digital economic base and institutions still organized by categories of the previous period, which contributes to the persistence of extraction mechanisms that are barely intelligible in the public sphere <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 8; p. 13)</2>.

In Dowbor, the “capture of flows” designates the transformation of digital circulation into a continuous economic asset: payments, data, attention and decisions cease to be side effects of use and come to form part of a measurable and monetizable flow, whose extraction depends on retaining enjoyment within controlled layers (accounts, permissions, proprietary standards, terms of use and curation), reducing the possibility of relevant use outside the governed perimeter <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-31)</2>.

The category reinforces that the consumption of IOC takes place as administered and continuously modulable access, and that the opacity of how this retention works projects duties of transparency and loyalty onto the material shaping of the offer (CDC), especially when legal-technical fences (including IP) are coupled to the perimeter to stabilize the capture <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 19-21; p. 28-31)</2>.

This command becomes capillary because “algorithms and artificial intelligence allow a capillarity that reaches every individual in the world” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>, shifting “consent” to a function that above all ratifies an arrangement already implemented, as can be glimpsed in the ordinary experience of compulsoriness: “I cannot move unless I am authorizing some network to install cookies all the time” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</4>.

In this key, the contract tends to operate as a subsequent discursive stabilization of a control already inscribed in the code, including in the administration of “access codes” and in the “management of contents” as structuring dimensions of the platform <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</2>.

When this practical normativity is articulated with technical fences and exclusivity regimes, the closing of access must be read in light of internal limits of legitimacy, above all when the effective teleology of the design shifts to a precarious and revocable toll regime over the enjoyment of IOCs <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 40)</2>.

According to Dowbor, the “nebulous reality” is not a spontaneous information deficit, but an institutional effect of the growing complexity of contemporary mediations for appropriating the surplus, which makes them less intelligible and, therefore, harder to politicize and to attribute in common understanding <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</2>.

The consequence is a practical blockage of collective response, associated with the picture of “institutional impotence”: “The institutional impotence we face leads us to a disastrous systemic disarticulation” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</2>.

At the same time, the author refuses to naturalize this opacity as a technical inevitability and makes its contestable character explicit when he states: “This book sets out to make visible and understandable how the mechanisms work today” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3)</2>.

In the sphere of platform consumption, this murkiness reinforces the insufficiency of merely formal transparency: the availability of terms, policies and documents does not remove the practical unintelligibility of the mechanism that organizes the capture and the toll embedded in the experience, which strains the reading of the duties of information, clarity and objective good faith under the CDC <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</2>.

Dowbor uses the formula “owner of a process” to indicate that, in digital rentierism, capture no longer depends on the alienation of a good and comes to stabilize through continued control of the conditions of use, converting enjoyment into authorized permanence within a governed circuit <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

On this view, the relevant economic object is not “content” as such, but the very operation of access — its permissions, compatibilities and criteria of continuity —, so that use becomes structurally conditional and subject to unilateral revision <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

The consequence is that the guarantees intuitively associated with acquisition lose practical density: availability, continuity and power of enjoyment come to depend on the holder of the infrastructure and on the private rules that administer the process <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

The architecture of access and enjoyment designates the set of technical and operational layers that sustain the utility of IOCs over time — code updates, authentication, server availability, compatibilities and integrations — and that therefore move consumption away from the logic of delivering a good toward continuous participation in a governed process <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>.

Dowbor describes this mutation as an institutional shift from a regime of producers and buyers to one of suppliers and users, and as the replacement of concrete property by recurring control of a process, in which economic capture is achieved by charging for use <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

Since enjoyment depends on these layers under the supplier's command, unilateral changes in maintenance, compatibility or access parameters may reconfigure the functional value delivered to the consumer — by degradation, locking or discontinuity — without the phenomenon being adequately captured by the classical categories of acquisition and permanence of the good <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>.

The reference to conditions of possibility is meant only to clarify that enjoyment of the immaterial depends on the supplier's infrastructural control over the practical regimes of access and circulation, so that the consumer's experience is structured by permissions and mediations controlled by the offeror — that is, by the administration of “access codes” and by the “management of content” as material dimensions of supply <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</2>.

For Dowbor, rentier enjoyment of the digital tends to be organized as authorized permanence in a process: access can be continuously conditioned and revised by the holder of the infrastructure, instead of being settled by the classical logic of delivering a good <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

This precariousness is not an episodic failure but a functional trait of the arrangement, since the supplier retains the capacity to restrict, reconfigure or end the experience through the administrative modulation of permissions, normalizing social life as a circuit of passage and recurring charges: “Living ceases to be a stroll […] to become a permanent race from toll to toll.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

Let us close the beaches, then. […] we are increasingly trapped in the race to increase our monthly income, without which we will find ourselves deprived of a series of essential services.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

Within the scope of the CDC, this reinforces that the signs “service”, “plan” and “purchase” may mask a structurally revocable enjoyment, increasing opacity and making it difficult, in practice, to anticipate and contest relevant changes in the conditions of use <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

In this sense, the author describes the corporate hardening of control as a “strategy implemented through a series of new laws intended to extend the copyright term of the work, reinforce criminal penalties for infringing copyright, and to punish the use of technologies that tried to circumvent the digital barriers placed on digital content” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 42-43)</2>.

The institutional effect is to convert the ordinary reproducibility of the digital into conditioned circulation: exclusion — through reinforced technical-legal fences — becomes the condition of possibility of the toll, that is, of the income extracted through control of access, and not through the social utility of dissemination <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22; p. 41; p. 51-52)</2>.

The “black box regime”, in the reading proposed from Dowbor, designates an institutional form of opacity in which relevant decisions are shifted to proprietary layers of calculation and organization — ranking, eligibility, visibility, balancing and availability — outside the user's ordinary intelligibility, in an environment marked by algorithmic capillarity and by the orientation of processing toward maximizing economic return <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

The practical consequence is evidentiary and cognitive: the consumer has neither intelligible traces nor a shared language with which to reconstruct the actual criteria for modulating the service, although they feel its effects directly in enjoyment <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

In such a context, even when formal terms and documents are available, transparency may remain insufficient for oversight and attribution, since the relevant decision-making mechanism remains unintelligible — a point that ties in with the diagnosis of growing complexity and opacity and with the insufficiency of merely formal transparency <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</2>.

Dowbor formulates the “inverted political sign” as a thesis of institutional reversibility: the same technical base that today sustains draining and enclosure can be organized for purposes of well-being and democratization, because the decisive vector is not “technology” in itself, but the arrangement of incentives and governance that structures access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 82)</2>.

The contrast emerges when the author observes that, while technology makes cultural goods more accessible, “the laws […] evolve symmetrically to make access ever more difficult”, moving the conflict to the legal and institutional regulation of enclosure <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 42)</2>.
Hence the conclusion that the “right of access to knowledge” becomes an axis of economic democratization <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 65)</2>.

This diagnosis finds a parallel in the treatment of network infrastructures and situations without effective competition, in which “private property and ‘economic freedom’, when there is no competition, lead to abuses”, that is, “it is private property, but not a market”, with loss of public purpose <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31-32)</2>.

This frame supports reading consumer protection law as bearing on the material shaping of the offer and of enjoyment in governed ecosystems, under requirements of transparency and loyalty that take account of the practical difficulty of reconciling profit and social purpose in hybrid structures <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 87)</2>.

Instead of appearing as public and comparable attributes of the offer, price and conditions become variables calculated per user, modulated by behavioral and socioeconomic inferences aimed at maximizing return <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

The Serasa example works as an institutionalized illustration of this rationality by recording that “your cost of credit will be adjusted according to the bank's interests”, showing that calibration may exploit information asymmetries and estimated needs, and not merely reflect “risk” in a neutral sense <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>.

In Dowbor's diagnosis, unproductive rentierism takes on a distributive expression when the proportionality between productive contribution and enrichment breaks down, consolidating itself as a drain on social wealth in favor of rentier positions; for the author, this shift marks the movement of the axis from capital accumulation to the logic of unproductive rentierism <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20)</2>.

The expression “communication corrals”, used by Dowbor, designates the infrastructural closure through which private operators come to control the conditions of access and circulation on the information highways themselves, consolidating the power to select, condition and administer enjoyment in proprietary environments <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49-50)</2>.

This closure cannot be reduced to a neutral technical choice, because it involves the coordinated appropriation of layers ranging from “physical infrastructure” to “codes” and “content”, moving the governance of the informational space into private regimes of passage <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49)</2>.

In an economic key, the “corrals” operate as the condition of possibility of recurring charges for access and permanence, since they transform circulation into an administered crossing and, therefore, one compatible with the toll rationality that runs through the diagnosis of contemporary rentierism <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 49-50)</2>.

The design can be read as compatible with the logic of toll and repeated micro-extraction described by Dowbor, insofar as it brings payment closer to a regime of small continuous captures that are barely salient to the individual <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29; p. 21)</2>.

When this closed circuit is combined with technical and contractual restrictions on circulation, the governance of access through turnstiles and crossing costs is reinforced, and this lies at the core of the diagnosis of toll and disproportionate extraction <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 39)</2>.
Thus, the informational rentierism described by Dowbor <1>(2024)</1> finds its microarchitectural correlate in the everyday life of platforms.

Intellectual property ceases to operate merely as an incentive and comes to form part of an arrangement of enclosure, functioning as a true “legal latifundium” that immobilizes accumulated technologies and knowledge under titles of prolonged exclusivity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>.

When this latifundium is coupled with license agreements, accounts, DRM, catalogs and authentication mechanisms, the incentive to create gives way to a technology of blocking and the purpose of copyright comes to operate as a mechanism for closing off access, turning access into a conditional license and enjoyment into a precarious, continuously reconfigurable authorization, insofar as circulation comes to be treated as infringement <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>.

The consequence, in the sphere of consumption, is that what gives concreteness to the consumer's right is not the possession of bits, but the legal materiality of the object, understood as the stability and predictability of the practical conditions that make enjoyment possible over time, in an environment in which economic control shifts from the good to the process and utility depends on continuous governance under private dominion <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

This is institutional concreteness, since the infrastructure and the mechanisms that sustain access, circulation and continuity remain under the control of platforms and their governance systems <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8; p. 51-52)</2>.

The decisive economic point is that, in the immaterial realm, reproducibility would tend to dissolve price, and this inversion is especially acute in the network environment, because copying is not a deviation but an ordinary technical condition of enjoyment itself, insofar as copying is part of transmission, storage, caching and, in a certain sense, reading itself <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

By legally requalifying this constitutive gesture, intellectual property ceases to operate merely as an incentive and comes to function as a technology of blocking, since it transforms circulation into infringement and enjoyment into authorization, allowing the supplier to govern the experience of the IOC as precarious and modulable access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

Dowbor describes the economic centrality of this surplus when he follows Gorz in analyzing the brand, advertising and symbolic values as the basis of a new formation of value <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2>.

Dowbor associates the problem of Intellectual Property not only with the existence of the right itself, but with its historical extension through organized pressure, observing that “we will only have digital access to a work 70 years after the author's death” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2> and questioning whether very long copyrights and “indefinitely extended” rights are disseminating culture or, on the contrary, stalling the social process <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</4>.

The argument is one of political economy, since, if profit is realized mostly in the first years of commercial exploitation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>, keeping exclusivity for decades operates as income without a proportional incentive function and imposes a massive social cost on research and creative reuse in order to sustain concentrated private flows.
The author, as the subject of intellectual creation, has little to do with this dynamic, since the rights almost always belong to intermediaries <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>.

Dowbor makes explicit that the proliferation and overlapping of IP rights may produce prohibitive transaction costs and block subsequent innovation by “placing multiple obstacles” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 47)</2>, amounting to a tragedy of the anticommons.

The thesis draws on examples that make the social materiality of this blocking explicit, citing the “disaster of access to vaccines during Covid-19” as evidence of the patent latifundium <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.
The attempt to patent the “one-click” mechanism is also mentioned, as a deliberate move to prevent the spread of a basic organizational improvement <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22-23)</2>.
In this process, availability, compatibility and continuity depend on external controls under the supplier's command <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>.

The architecture of cumulative permissions comes close to the diagnosis that tangles of legal restrictions and transaction costs may produce underuse and blockages through an excess of vetoes, to the detriment of recombination and subsequent innovation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44; p. 47)</2>, and helps explain why economic activity comes to depend on persistent legal mediations even in trivial operations of production and circulation <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 45-46)</4>.

For this reason, he reaffirms public access to knowledge as a structuring vector, maintaining that knowledge generated with public resources must be socially accessible and serve the common good, and that access to knowledge and connectivity today constitutes a fundamental human right <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 62)</2>.

Along the same lines, he states that copyright must be limited, since its purpose is to ensure reasonable remuneration for the author, not to guarantee permanent income to the intermediary, which is why he proposes a time limit, possibly on the order of five years <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

Intermediaries and chains of exploitation remain remunerable, but capture must occur through mechanisms compatible with circulation and access, and not through permanent tolls <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 64)</2>.

On the contrary, he recognizes the historical legitimacy of the incentive, understood as privileged remuneration of the inventor or the author, so as to stimulate scientific and cultural advances <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

On this view, patents and copyrights no longer operate predominantly as a temporary technique of stimulus and come to function as a mechanism of blocking and toll over knowledge, including when effective ownership shifts to intermediaries and economic groups <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36; p. 43; p. 46)</2>.
Intellectual property rights are not based on a natural right of property, but on their potential to stimulate future creativity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

It follows that the hypertrophy of duration and scope produces a teleological mismatch and calls for proportionality review when exclusivity becomes detached from the incentive and comes to operate as a fence <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

The metaphor of the “legal latifundium”, in Dowbor, describes a teleological dysfunction internal to the Intellectual Property regime: situations in which exclusivity, through hypertrophy of scope, duration and chains of licenses, ceases to operate predominantly as a temporary technique for stimulating future creativity and comes to function as a mechanism for the artificial retention of social utility and for charging tolls on access, recombination and dissemination of technically reproducible knowledge <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44-45)</2>.

The critique therefore does not deny IP as a legal technique, but traces its legitimacy back to the purposive foundation the author makes explicit: “The intellectual property right is not based on the natural right of property, but on its potential to stimulate future creativity.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

The dysfunction worsens when appropriation systematically shifts from the creator to intermediaries, composing the figure of the “absentee owner”: “Copyrights are largely taken over by those who hold the copyright or the patents, and in this case they are almost always intermediaries.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

In this scenario, the title of exclusivity tends to operate as an economic and institutional bottleneck in the final product, conditioning subsequent trajectories of innovation and access on private control of permissions and licenses, with potential for disproportionate enrichment by position in the circuit <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48-49; p. 58)</2>.

In Dowbor, “fence” designates the teleological turn in which copyright ceases to operate predominantly as an incentive and comes to function as a perimeter barring access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>, linked to the general mechanism of converting the reproducibility of the immaterial into monetizable artificial scarcity, that is, turning technical abundance into scarcity by institutional decision <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</4>.

The utility of the immaterial object depends on the governed continuity of access and on the stability of the technical-organizational rules that structure availability, compatibility and modification, and not on the digital medium itself <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

The structural point is that this stability is anchored in infrastructures under private control, so that the “productive infrastructure […] is controlled by platforms, computers, algorithms and artificial intelligence”. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</2>.

For this reason, the instability of these rules reconfigures, in practice, the functional value delivered to the consumer and makes enjoyment dependent on continuous governance as a process <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

Dowbor locates the corresponding shift by following Gorz, noting that “Gorz naturally moves on to analyze the function of the brand, advertising, symbolic values as the basis of the new formation of value” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2> and that, in the contemporary mutation, “The theory of value, the basis of economic science, shifts” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</4>, toward a regime in which exchange value is anchored “mainly, by its content of knowledge, information, general intelligence” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</6>.

On this view, the institutional problem is not symbolic circulation as such, but the possibility of its capture by contractual and IP fences and by asymmetric governance of visibility and access, turning diffuse contribution back into an exclusive asset and recurring income; the logic of the “bottleneck” and the “toll” imposed on socially cumulative accumulations provides the structural model of this appropriation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48-49)</2>.

In this scenario, the user's contribution no longer operates as a communal element that deepens enjoyment and comes to be requalified as a proprietary input, which ties in with Dowbor's diagnosis of the reorganization of value formation around brand, advertising and symbolic values <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2> and of the dependence, in the immaterial realm, on institutional mechanisms that block dissemination in order to stabilize monetization <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 41)</4>.

If exclusivity is legitimized by its instrumental function of stimulating future creativity, extending control beyond the typical period for recouping the investment tends to reduce the marginal incentive gain and to operate as continued income by position <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

In the case of copyright, the author observes that profits are realized mostly in the first cycles of exploitation, whereas legal exclusivity may last for decades, converting the remaining protection into a barrier to access, with significant social costs for cultural dissemination, recombination and licensing, without a proportional benefit in new creations <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

This asymmetry reinforces the need to read the social function of IP, in platform environments, as a criterion for containing enclosures that come to operate as a toll on technically facilitated circulation, shifting the discussion from the isolated “title” to the institutional architecture that produces blocking, opacity and capture of value in the intangible <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43; p. 46)</2>.

Dowbor draws on Boyle's synthesis to record this effect as a “tragedy of the anticommons”, associating it with the transaction costs generated by a “myriad” of property rights and with the result of restricting innovation by placing multiple obstacles in the path of subsequent developments <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 47)</2>, a diagnosis reinforced by the idea that the “tangle of legal restrictions” may reach a point at which it “hinders more than it stimulates research” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</4>.

The “patent latifundium” makes it possible to show, by way of example, the loss of proportionality between exclusivity and the corresponding social benefit when barriers persist even under collective urgency: in Dowbor's diagnosis, the “disaster of access to vaccines during Covid-19” exposes how patents can “immobilize” essential technology and organize a “war to make access difficult” as an income mechanism, including under shareholder pressure for dividends to the detriment of access pacts <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36; p. 54)</2>.

The example is useful because it shows that exclusivity may become detached from its justification and operate as a social and economic toll on dissemination, access and the capacity for public response, reinstating the social function of IP as a criterion of institutional limitation and calibration <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

Dowbor, on the one hand, observes that “openness itself has become a powerful (and impressively beneficial) incentive” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 38)</2> and, on the other, maintains that remuneration can be organized at another point in the economic chain, preventing long and hypertrophied exclusivities from turning into a permanent toll <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 64)</4>.

Within this horizon, several institutional arrangements that the law can accommodate come into view, including funding policies and public procurement, in which remuneration occurs through distributive and public policy mechanisms, consistent with the role of collectively funded basic science and with the circulation of the result as a common good without prejudice to payment for creative work <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 6; p. 39)</2>; remunerated compulsory licenses and sectoral flexibilities as an exceptional technique to overcome bottlenecks and enable technology transfer in the face of global challenges, including solutions such as pools and access-oriented flexibilities <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 53)</4>; and open licensing models and collective forms of management, which reduce transaction costs and avoid systemic blockages by shifting remuneration to services, curation, maintenance and complementary activities <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43-44; p. 64)</6>.

Taken together, the instruments show that IP, read through its social function, admits degrees of exclusivity and instruments of teleological correction when hypertrophied exclusivity comes to operate as a structural barrier to cultural circulation, recombination and public access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43-44; p. 64)</2>.

Dowbor recognizes the historical justification of intellectual protection as a technique of incentive — privileged remuneration of the inventor and the author to stimulate scientific and cultural advances —, but maintains that, in the contemporary configuration, patents and copyrights tend to operate as a rentier mechanism of charging for access and blocking the dissemination of knowledge <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

The author illustrates the dysfunction with the patent's temporal mismatch with the pace of technology, pointing to the Covid-19 pandemic as a case of socially disastrous restriction of access, and with the expansion of copyright and its economic concentration in publishers rather than authors, citing the prospect that the works of Paulo Freire will enter open access only in 2067 <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

In this diagnosis, the “war to make access difficult” becomes a central axis of the knowledge economy, while openness mechanisms (Open Access, Creative Commons and the like) appear as an institutional alternative capable of radically expanding worldwide access to knowledge without depending on retention as the ordinary form of remuneration <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

ACOSTA, Leonardo Machado. <1>Cibervulnerabilidade: </1>a vulnerabilidade agravada dos consumidores no ciberespaço. 2025. 137 f. Dissertação (Mestrado em Direito) – Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp), Faculdade de Ciências Humanas e Sociais, Franca, 2025.

The notion of “cybervulnerability” rightly registers that cyberspace aggravates known vulnerabilities and widens the power gap between consumer and supplier, through factors such as insufficient literacy, informational asymmetry, data collection and the manipulation of will <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 86; p. 93; p. 97; p. 120; p. 83-84)</2>.

The author does seek to give the notion legal footing through the CDC and the Constitution, which shows a serious normative effort, but the formulation still relies heavily on “cyberspace” as its structural axis <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 93; p. 113; p. 119)</2>.

Along these lines, the author defines “cybervulnerability” as “the hypervulnerability of the consumer caused by the greater fragility of this subject in consumer relations established in cyberspace given the existence of more uncertainties, risks and occurrences of harm in this environment, which increases the power gap between the consumer and the supplier” <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 86)</2>.

Acosta maintains that cybervulnerability results from the “aggravation of the consumer's vulnerability(ies) caused by the insertion and action of this agent within cyberspace” <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 86)</2>, and stresses that it is a form of hypervulnerability arising from the sum of vulnerabilities beyond the usual, which stem from the characteristics of this environment <3>Acosta</3><4>(Acosta, 2025, p. 93)</4>.

Chief among them is aggravated technical vulnerability, associated with two central circumstances: a structural one, linked to the very architecture of the virtual environment, and a situational one, related to the cognitive and behavioral effects of using this medium, both of which further weaken the consumer in relations established digitally <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 97)</2>.

In addition, he makes explicit other concrete factors that deepen this picture, such as the informational power gap, the lack of digital literacy, the indiscriminate collection and processing of personal data and the manipulation of individuals' will <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 120)</2>.

In an especially illuminating passage, the author describes how the digital market tends to make the provision of services conditional on data collection, with the data later stored and processed by algorithms designed to shape will, whether through behavioral advertising or through broader forms of steering decisions in favor of companies or other centers of power that control these informational bases <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 83-84)</2>.

The author insists on the need to establish a concept and parameters grounded in the principles of the Consumer Protection Code and the Federal Constitution, precisely to allow effective protection and guarantee material equality to consumers operating in cyberspace <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 93)</2>.

This appears when the author acknowledges the precariousness, indeed near absence, of legal protection specifically aimed at the “cybervulnerable”, which hinders the direct application of protective rules within the Brazilian legal system and makes the search for provisional interpretive solutions inevitable <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 113)</2>.

The same tension reappears when he advocates, for the future, specific regulation that recognizes and combats the aggravated vulnerabilities of cyberspace, while for the present he relies on interpretation favorable to the consumer based on the CDC and the Constitution <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 119)</2>.

The seminal article by Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis <1>([201-?])</1>, The Right to Privacy, originally published in the Harvard Law Review in 1890, sets out a matrix for legal reconstruction in the face of technical and social changes that alter the conditions of exposure, vulnerability and harm.

Turning to Brandeis <1>(2011)</1> at this point structurally reinforces the diagnosis already established of the Lex Plataformae as practical normativity, avoiding both the moralization of private power and the leap to state control.

In the arrangement Brandeis describes, domination does not take the form of a formal public command, but of gradual control over essential circuits and of the capacity to coordinate decisions by administering other people's money <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 27])</2>.

On this account, decisive influence arises not from wealth itself, but from the capacity to command other people's resources and thereby direct economic conduct and trajectories <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 37])</2>.

Brandeis describes how distinct functions indispensable to business end up combined in the figure of the investment banker, and attributes the formation of the Money Trust to this combination <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 26-27])</2>.

From there, the historical form of the phenomenon becomes comparable to that of political despotism, since it takes hold through progressive usurpation, advancing incrementally rather than through violent acts of rupture <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 26-27])</2>.

Brandeis is explicit about the requirement that banking be kept separate from the business it finances, because combining the functions produces a structural conflict of interest <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 196])</2>.

The author describes this kind of rationality by showing how decision-makers may guide their action by its probable effect on market value, constantly attentive to how investors and the street will read the facts <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 200])</2>.

Louis D. Brandeis's Other People’s Money and How the Bankers Use It <1>(2011)</1>, originally published between 1913 and 1914 as a series of articles in Harper’s Weekly, is a structural critique of the formation of a financial oligarchy in the early twentieth century. What matters here is solely the characterization of the legal and institutional mechanism Brandeis describes.

The point is not merely “one director on two boards”, but the network of ties that lets decisions and contracts run through crossed circuits, reducing independence in decision-making and blurring fiduciary loyalties <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 67])</2>.

For him, when bigness is achieved through combinations and mergers and comes to be managed remotely, the result tends to be a concentration of power with poorer decisions and a practical inability to govern operational complexity without degradation, which turns “bigness” into a source of inefficiency and systemic risk <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 166])</2>.

In Brandeis, functional encroachment designates the way a financial oligarchy consolidates itself not through a single act of conquest, but through gradual, discreet and often barely visible usurpation, which progressively shifts to one group functions that, when exercised separately, tend to produce reciprocal checks and competitive balance <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 25-28])</2>.

The information society itself, by intensifying private structures of surveillance and behavioral analysis, required new fundamental rights to be made explicit and data protection to be reinforced in response to the practical erosion of privacy <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69-70; p. 78-79; p. 82- 83)</2>.

The point is to recognize that private structures of digital governance bear on privacy, personality, freedom and self-determination intensely enough to justify reinforced legal containment <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141; p. 152; p. 155)</2>.

Along the same lines, massive data exploitation, behavioral analysis and corporate surveillance show that these private powers now operate over central spheres of autonomy to a constitutionally relevant degree, calling for a more robust normative response <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70; p. 72; p. 78)</2>.

Along these lines, data protection imposes a true obligation on the processing agent to respect the data subject's informational self-determination, precisely because personal data constitute an extension of their personality, protected by the constitutional centrality of human dignity <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155)</2>.

The same key appears in the statement that guaranteeing the protection of personal data, whether through the LGPD or through the horizontal effect of fundamental rights in the concrete case, especially those tied to privacy and personality, ultimately aims to protect the fundamental rights of the data subject <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 156)</2>.

For this reason, the statutory protection of personal data can be understood as an expression of the indirect horizontal effect of the fundamental rights of freedom, privacy and free development of the natural person, opening room for these principles to bear more directly on private relations <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 156)</2>.

Along these lines, the development of information and communication technologies, in a surveillance society marked by the mitigation of privacy, imposed the need to reflect on new fundamental rights <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69-70)</2>.

The same key is reinforced by the recognition that the economic exploitation of personal data without sufficient consent did not remain a matter of ordinary legislation alone, since STF case law has confirmed the existence of autonomous fundamental rights to the protection of personal data and to informational self-determination <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 82-83)</2>.

In addition, these rights are understood as the result of an evolutive interpretation of privacy, whose protection had to be reconfigured to remain effective in the surveillance society <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 78-79)</2>.

In this direction, the protection of personality rights does not end with their enactment in the Civil Code, since they also have the stature of fundamental rights, which allows data protection itself to be understood as a way of defending these rights <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 152)</2>.

The same reasoning is reinforced when the problem is placed within the tension between an impersonal market and the protection of the fundamental rights of the natural person exposed to such influences, from the perspective of a repersonalization of private law <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141)</2>.

Where vulnerability is justifiable, the fundamental norm may even be applied directly, in its pure form, to bring about an effective rebalancing between the parties <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155)</2>.

In a surveillance society, the enormous amount of personal data converted into information about personality and intimacy, and used by companies for behavioral analysis, calls into question whether privacy can be preserved at all <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>.

This reading deepens with the recognition, in dialogue with Shoshana Zuboff, that the power derived from extracting and analyzing personal data extends to the capacity to shape human behavior, calling for responses that contain and regulate surveillance capitalism <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 72)</2>.

In addition, the existence of abuses committed by technology companies reinforces the need for more robust protection of data processing relations, including in digital media <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 78)</2>.

In the digital environment, the storage, sharing and persistent monitoring of information pose a threat to privacy serious enough to require specific normative containment, above all in a surveillance society in which data processing becomes a central asset of business models and behavioral control <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69; p. 73; p. 82)</2>.

The security argument itself may serve to legitimize the expansion of private powers over fundamental spheres of informational life, especially when data demands and structural surveillance are normalized through routine and barely intelligible acceptances <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70-71)</2>.

In the digital environment, the constant storage and sharing of information pose a serious threat to fundamental rights, especially privacy, requiring more specific regulatory action to curb abuses of this kind <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69)</2>.

The same key is reinforced when contemporary society is described as a true surveillance society, permanently geared to data collection, which explains the need to regulate digital relations with a focus on protecting personal data, privacy and other fundamental rights affected by this technological medium <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 73)</2>.

In addition, the processing of personal data has become the main asset of a hyperconnected society, serving as raw material for improving businesses and extracting behavioral patterns used to classify and categorize people, which is why the law seeks to keep pace with this development through new legislation and new rights that safeguard fundamental rights <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 82)</2>.

In the aftermath of the September 11 attack, a gradual erosion of privacy and other fundamental guarantees took hold in the name of a growing need for transparency, opening the way for companies to collect, select and classify personal data in order to control individuals <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>.

The same logic appears when access to platforms and websites is often made conditional on entering personal data, frequently without the data subject's genuinely informed consent, and those data are later exploited commercially and monetized through advertising and other business models <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>.

Moreover, automated processing does not merely know human behavior but shapes it at scale, so that the goal is no longer only to automate the flow of information about people but comes to include automating people themselves <1>Mendes</1><2>(Zuboff apud Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 71)</2>.

The digital experience may reach legally relevant dimensions of personal integrity precisely because data protection, informational self-determination and the free development of personality belong to the existential core of the person in the informational environment <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 139; p. 148; p. 155-156)</2>.

Today, this means recognizing that so-called digital dossiers constitute a new type of identity and that personal data are bound up with the free exercise and development of human personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141; p. 153)</2>.

Along these lines, the specific protection of personal data appears as a means of guaranteeing established fundamental rights, such as freedom and privacy, as well as more recently developed ones, including informational self-determination and the free development of personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 139)</2>.

This connection deepens with the statement that informational self-determination serves precisely the free development of the data subject's personality, which is why any interpretation that distorts it, for example through unrestricted consent harmful to that development, must be deemed unacceptable <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 148)</2>.

Moreover, informational self-determination and the centrality of the data subject appear as means of strengthening the natural person's free self-determination and free development of personality, giving them the tools to control how their data are processed, including confirmation that processing exists, correction, modification and deletion <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155-156)</2>.

In this context, the repersonalization of private law brings back to the center the tension between the demands of an impersonal, economically driven market and the need to protect the fundamental rights of the natural person exposed to external influences <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141)</2>.

This reading gains depth with the recognition that data processing increasingly intrudes on people's lives and that so-called digital dossiers constitute a “new type of identity”, which is why correcting this information becomes essential for the data subject's identity to be projected faithfully, providing the doctrinal justification for placing personal data in the category of personality rights <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 153)</2>.

Moreover, personal data are described as a “true extension of the free exercise and development of human personality”, so that informational self-determination rests not on mere ownership of data but on its inseparable relation to the data subject's personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 153)</2>.

Warat makes this core explicit when he treats the semiology of power as an analysis of how signification can function as an instrument of social control, a normalizing and disciplinary strategy and a consensus-producing formula, capable of fabricating effects of verisimilitude about the material conditions of social life <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 18)</2>.

In objective terms, the author maintains that the legitimacy of power depends on discursive work and can be obtained through the right handling of words, which moves the appearance of publicity and formal validity to the level of its strategic production <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 18)</2>.

This operation is reinforced by the recognition that the stability of meaning rests on a prior ideological coincidence, so that belief in normative univocity and in the unalterability of signifiers does not stem from naivety but works as a condition for the social effectiveness of the ideal of the rational legal norm <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 68)</2>.

For this reason, obedience can be produced without an explicit command, since the social idiom tends to constitute an ordered subjectivity, making it possible to dispense with physical violence and convert it into significative or imaginary violence, through which social cohesion is maintained by creating phantasmatic significations <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 110)</2>
Luis Alberto Warat's O Direito e sua Linguagem <1>(1984)</1> introduces the problem of language in law head-on, rejecting the idea that legal discourse operates as a neutral instrument of naming.

It is through its ‘devices of signification’ that power disciplines bodies, causing the members of a society to bind their desires to power. […] The ‘social idiom’ ends up constituting an ‘ordered subjectivity’ […] that allows physical violence to be progressively dispensed with, transformed into ‘significative violence’, into ‘imaginary violence’. […] Society keeps itself cohesive by resorting to the creation of phantasmatic significations […]” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 110)</2>.

It is in this key that signification can be analyzed as an instrument of social control, normalization and consensus production, and not merely as a neutral vehicle of information <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>.
Hence the case for abandoning environmental labels in favor of categories that isolate the actual mechanism by which meaning is produced <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 15; p. 47)</2>.

Warat is explicit in stating that signification must be analyzed “as an instrument of social control”, “as a normalizing and disciplinary strategy of individuals”, “as a consensus-producing formula” and “as a persuasive power provoking effects of verisimilitude about the material conditions of social life” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>.

For the author, languages are not limited to the informative content they apparently transmit; they engender “significative and normalizing resonances of social practices”, inserting themselves into a deeper dynamic of “social production of meanings” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 15)</2>.

In a convergent sense, Warat observes that pragmatic analysis makes it possible to articulate functions such as “persuasion, legitimation, anticipation”, showing how certain discourses produce an “effect of unquestionability and reality about knowledge” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</2>.

Pragmatics applied to law reveals that ideology is “a factor inseparable from the conceptual structure made explicit in general norms”, requiring the interpreter to read in a way that uncovers “the connections between the words of the law and the political and ideological factors that produce and determine its functions in society” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</2>.

Normative discourses involve a “game of persuasion and mythification” that stereotypes meanings and legitimizes the reproduction of power under the appearance of normality <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 45)</2>.

Through the use of “a language impregnated with stereotyped significations”, “an ideological dimension not formulated in legal language” is introduced “under the supposed appearance of an objective description”, the central aim of these expressions being “to influence and determine opinions” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 71)</2>.

The “coherent organization of a discourse” can “silence problems” and, through these silences, fulfill “political functions in society”, at the same time as it “explicitly forces subjects to say or repress certain things” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 50)</2>.

This selectivity is reinforced when legal discourse presents itself under the appearance of univocity and closure: belief in normative univocity presupposes “prior ideological coincidence” and the unalterability of signifiers sustains the ideal of a rational norm precisely because it ensures certain “social effects of the law in society” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 68)</2>.

The critique of the claim that legal language is closed shows that the system's demands for totality and closure are not mere logical requirements, but ideological representations that serve specific functions of the legal form <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 54)</2>.

Consensus on the legitimacy of power is the result of discursive work, which is effective precisely because it operates through “a game of stereotyping”, whose primary function is legitimation <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>.

In this situation, physical violence becomes largely dispensable, replaced by “significative violence” and “imaginary violence”, which can neutralize the critical power of subjectivity and produce internalized obedience <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 110)</2>.

Certain effects of acceptance spread without any need for explicit demonstration, relying on stereotypes, topical formulas and settled beliefs, so that discursive alignment spreads “like an infection” or “contagion” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 88)</2>.

The author warns that the function of domination should not be analyzed “from a psychologistic point of view”, since senders and receivers are institutionally situated and their discourses serve as carriers of a mediatized ideology <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 67)</2>.

This key is reinforced when Warat shows that whoever produces the discourse can secure “the monopoly of the constitution of the denotative field”, selecting designative properties for persuasive ends and leaving receivers “dormant to the discussion of the persuasively proposed designative criteria” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 70)</2>.

POSTMAN, Neil. <1>Amusing ourselves to death:</1> public discourse in the age of show business. New introduction by Andrew Postman. 20th anniversary ed. New York: Penguin Books, 2006.
Neil Postman's contribution <1>(2006)</1>, influenced by Ellul, moves the diagnosis of technique to the plane of media as the dominant cultural form.

Politics, religion and education come to operate under the grammar of entertainment, in a society that approaches the condition of “amusing ourselves to death” <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</2>.

In the political field, visual logic shifts the weight of argument to appearance, performance and impression management, reducing the centrality of programs, ideologies and substantive confrontations of ideas <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</2>.
In the religious domain, television tends to convert the experience of transcendence into spectacle, emptying ritual density and symbolic depth <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</2>.

In education, a pedagogical philosophy guided by immediate accessibility and gratification takes hold, at the expense of cognitive effort and more demanding intellectual formation <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 96])</2>.
Postman <1>(2006)</1> makes it possible to understand media as a way of organizing social knowledge, and not merely as a channel through which messages circulate.

The shift from typographic culture to television did not merely change the medium of communication; it transformed the criteria of truth, intelligence and seriousness in public discourse <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 23])</2>.

Under this regime, television favors fragmentation, narrows the room for more complex discourse and replaces the argumentative coherence of typographic culture with public conversation marked by triviality, broken sequence and the gradual abandonment of logic, reason and the rules of contradiction <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58])</2>.
For Postman, television reconfigures it as a branch of show business, transforming public debate into a product compatible with entertainment <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</2>.
In this context, “knowing” politics comes to mean visual familiarity, and not necessarily understanding structured by language and discourse <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 86])</2>.

Critical, in-depth engagement gives way to recreational forms of access to content, while difficulty, intellectual discipline and sustained cognitive effort come to be seen as obstacles to efficient communication <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 146])</2>.

Hence the claim that television and image culture are not merely a style of communication but a threat to the foundations of liberal democracy, insofar as they strike at its material basis: freedom of information <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 91])</2>.

The image dismembers reality by wrenching moments out of their contexts and juxtaposing events with no logical or historical connection, recreating the world as a series of idiosyncratic occurrences <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 55])</2>.

In this environment, intelligence comes to mean knowing of many things, and not knowing about them, that is, accumulating disconnected data without in-depth understanding <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 74])</2>.

Disinformation, therefore, cannot be reduced to falsehood; since it also takes the form of misplaced, irrelevant, fragmented or superficial information, capable of producing an illusion of knowledge and drawing the subject away from genuine knowing <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 74])</2>.

This way of circulating information produces a present without historicity, in which television operates as a medium centered on the now and makes it hard to integrate experience into a broader temporal narrative <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 76])</2>.

Public discourse thus loses the form that made it fit for rationality: under print culture, it tended toward coherence, seriousness and continuity; under televisual governance, it comes to be organized by visuality, brevity and the demand for immediate interest <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 65-66])</2>.

Information is presented in simplified, insubstantial and decontextualized form, not necessarily through explicit censorship, but because television operates as a meta-medium, directing both what is known of the world and the social ways of knowing <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58])</2>.

Following this change of foundation, politics, religion, news, education and commerce come to be rearranged as congenial adjuncts of show business, and culture tends to turn into a generalized arena of entertainment <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58-59])</2>.

Read this way, the contemporary threat to democracy need not take the form of censorship, since it materializes when political discourse takes the form of entertainment and neutralizes the very seriousness of public debate <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 91-93])</2>.

By moving the center of discourse to performance, the medium diminishes the public centrality of substantive issues and weakens the social conditions for critical thought, above all when information is presented in a simplistic, decontextualized way, that is, as information packaged as entertainment <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 92])</2>.

Influenced by the theory of Jacques Ellul, in Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business (“Divertindo-nos até a morte: o discurso público na era do show business”, in our translation), originally published in 1985, the American educator Neil Postman <1>(2006)</1> examines the influence of television on American culture, exploring the ways in which television, upon becoming the dominant medium of communication, turned public discourse into entertainment and profoundly affected the social, cultural and political epistemologies of the United States.

In the religious field, Postman maintains that television unceremoniously turns religion into entertainment, stripping away what made it a historical, profound and sacred practice, with the loss of ritual, dogma, tradition, theology and, above all, spiritual transcendence <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</2>.
In this format, preachers are no longer mere mediators and come to act as media protagonists, so that “their featured players become celebrities” <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 82])</2>.
The author describes this shift with explicit irony when he says that, in these programs, “the preacher is tops” and “God comes out as second banana” <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</2>.

God “exists only in our minds”, while the preacher is “there, to be seen, admired, adored”, becoming the star of the show under an essentially structural logic <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 83])</2>.

Postman's final contribution lies in a warning about the dangers of the "distracted society" that the communication mechanism had created, a concept that resonates forcefully in the contemporary context, in which the reality Postman <1>(2006)</1> observed has been raised exponentially by the introduction of new digital communication technologies that merely intensified and amplified the dynamics the author had observed.
